text: Read each problem fully before starting. Where's the crux? Where will you rest?
Place every foot so silently that no sound is audible. If your foot makes noise, retry the placement.
Focus on shoulder engagement — active hang, not passive. Depress and retract your scapulae before every rep.
Quality over quantity — stop the set when form breaks down. A sloppy rep teaches bad patterns.
Count your breaths at every rest position. Breathing rhythm is the foundation of route climbing endurance.
G-Tox: while resting on the wall, alternate your arms — overhead for 5s, then down at your side for 5s. Gravity helps clear metabolites faster.
Between hard attempts, do 2-3 minutes of easy traversing instead of sitting. Active recovery promotes faster reperfusion than passive rest.
Before each climb, scan the route bottom to top for 30 seconds. Identify rest spots, the crux, and your clipping positions.
Today's focus: hip rotation. On every move, think about turning your hips toward the wall before reaching.
Hover your hand 2cm above the target hold for a full second before grabbing. This prevents lunging and builds precision.
Downclimb every warm-up problem back to the start. It builds eccentric strength and route-reading in reverse.
If you feel ANY pump during ARC, you're going too hard. Drop the grade. The goal is blood flow, not effort.
Rest day tomorrow is part of the plan, not a break from it. Adaptation happens during recovery, not during training.
Squeeze every rep with maximal intent. On hangboard, the difference between 90% effort and 100% effort is the difference between maintenance and adaptation.
Try flagging on every move today, even where it's not strictly necessary. Building the habit makes it automatic when you need it.
Pause 2-3 seconds after each move. No dynamic movements. Feel your body position before reaching for the next hold.
Warm up your fingers progressively — never go from cold to max. Your pulleys need time to reach full physiological slack.
On conditioning exercises, focus on full range of motion. Half reps build half strength.
Use open-hand grip whenever possible on the hangboard. Save your crimp for the wall where you actually need it.
Shake out each arm for 10 seconds between sets. Blood flow is your friend — help it do its job.
Today is deload — resist the temptation to go hard. Your body is consolidating gains from the last phase. Trust the process.
Engage your core before every dynamic move. A split second of tension through your midsection transfers power from feet to hands.
Eccentric control wins. On every pull-up, lower yourself in 3-4 seconds. The descent builds more strength than the ascent.
Stare at the foothold for 2 seconds after placing your foot. This builds precision and trust in your placements.
Breathe. Exhale on the hardest part of each move. Holding your breath increases blood pressure and wastes energy.
Read the entire problem before you start. Where are the holds, where is the crux, where can you rest?
source: Seifert 2017 (preview improves fluency; experts use sequence-of-blocks strategy)

text: One full-intensity attempt, then rest completely. Neural recovery between limit attempts needs 3-5 minutes.
Walk between attempts — don't sit down. Active rest accelerates lactate clearance by ~35%.
Visualize the full sequence before each attempt — include the effort sensation, not just positions. Watch your mental movie at least 3 times as often as you climb.
Focus on the process, not the grade. Movement quality reduces anxiety and improves motor learning.
If your foot cuts, ask why — body tension or placement? Distinguishing the error type guides your next correction.
Scale the warm-up: 15-20 minutes progressive, never a cold start. Flash pump prevention requires a gradual ramp.
After 5 attempts on the same boulder, switch problems. Diminishing neural returns and tendon overuse risk — come back next session with fresh fingers.
In volume sessions, stay 2-3 grades below your max — seek flow, not fight. Volume is a technical-metabolic stimulus, not a neural one.
No heavy static forearm stretching before climbing — it can reduce grip strength for up to an hour. Light stretching and Armaid are fine.
Log sleep, fueling, and fatigue before starting. Numbers without context aren't data — they're noise you'll trust by mistake.
Ramp the warm-up gradually — light loads, never to failure. The first max attempt must feel fresh, not pre-fatigued.
Rest 5+ minutes between max attempts — neural recovery isn't optional. Rushing back wastes the rep and biases the score low.
Drive the thumb pad into the long pinch — full contact, neutral wrist. Compromising the wrist for 'feel' wastes the rep.
Pace the repeater — don't blow early sets chasing reps. The score is your sustainable capacity, not your rep-one bravado.
Full extension at the bottom, chin clearly over the bar at the top. Half-reps and kips don't count toward your score.
Once form breaks, the rep doesn't count — and the next won't either. Stop while the data is still clean.
Breathe slowly and let the day's tension dissolve — this isn't a flexibility contest. The work is the unwinding.
Hold each static stretch ≥30 seconds — never push to pain. Three calm sessions beat one intense one for tissue adaptation.
Stack from ground up — wrist, shoulder, hip, heel. Correct every three breaths; falls are reps, not failures.
Move antagonist work at slow tempo — three up, three down. The unsexy work is what keeps you climbing past thirty-five.
Take one planned fall each session — small, above the bolt, eyes open. Fear shrinks when the body owns the experience.
Pre-read every clip — which hold, which hand, which body position. Clipping from a struggle is lead's costliest error.
Long exhale through pump — 4 seconds out, slow in. The slow exhale interrupts the panic loop driven by rising CO₂.
Call the clip, the take, the fall — silent climbers stress belayers, and stressed belayers shorten rope at the worst moment.
Between attempts, close your eyes and replay the sequence for 60 seconds. Recall builds motor learning faster than another try.
Between climbs, ten scapular pushups or band external rotations. Antagonist work keeps shoulders packed and balances pulling.
Past the 60-minute mark, take 20–30g of carbs — banana, gel, dates. Glycogen drop after an hour eats final-attempt quality.
File skin smooth before it tears; once damage control begins, call the session. You don't get the lost friction back today.
Hold every hangboard rep in clean half-crimp — that grip is your contract with your tendons. Drifts mid-rep are warning signs.
Drop the weight before you drop form. The strength that transfers to climbing is the strength produced cleanly.
Brace before each set — exhale, lock the pelvis, then move. A loose core under load leaks the tension your hardest moves need.
On short repeater sets, treat pump as feedback, not enemy. End the set when grip shape changes — that's when the data goes bad.
After general warm-up, add five minutes of low-load grip-pattern primers. Cold tissue under max load is the injury setup.
During deload, walk and move easy daily — sedentary rest slows the blood flow that delivers adaptation. Easy is not stop.
